**Explanation:**
The story is highly original in both its prose and its execution of plot. It avoids overused expressions in favor of specific, fresh imagery and observations (e.g., a nurse attaching a baby to a breast "with the practical confidence of someone attaching a vacuum-cleaner accessory," or Ben announcing the birth time "in the voice he used when identifying a bird"). 

Furthermore, while the premise of "babies switched at birth" is a known trope, the author completely subverts the cliché. Instead of the predictable reaction of panic, tears, and rushing back to the nurses' station to demand her biological daughter, Clara experiences a surreal, quiet epiphany of "immense happiness" and consciously chooses to walk out of the hospital with the baby boy. It also actively deconstructs the cliché of instant, mystical maternal recognition, noting that Clara had been told there would be "a knowledge older than thought," when in reality she only felt a non-specific tenderness she might have felt "for any small animal awake beneath fluorescent lights."
